Part 1: Genealogies in Luke and Matthew

The genealogies in Luke and Matthew appear to briefly converge at Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel. However, they differ both above Shealtiel and below Zerubbabel. Matthew's genealogy departs from the Old Testament record at this point. In the Old Testament, Zerubbabel was a hero who led the Jews back from Babylon, governed Judah, and rebuilt the temple. He is called a son of Shealtiel several times in the Old Testament. There is a discrepancy in the Book of Chronicles, where Zerubbabel's father is given as Shealtiel in the Septuagint text, but as Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother, in the Masoretic text. Most scholars accept the Septuagint reading as original.

Part 2: Critique of the Reformers

The critique of the Reformers is as follows:

"You complain of the doctrines and morals of the Reformers, applying the same critique you had made about public Scholastic disputations. Look around on this 'Evangelical' generation, and observe whether amongst them less indulgence is given to luxury, lust, or avarice, than amongst those whom you so detest. Show me any one person who by that Gospel has been reclaimed from drunkenness to sobriety, from fury and passion to meekness, from avarice to liberality, from reviling to well-speaking, from wantonness to modesty. I will show you a great many who have become worse through following it. ...The solemn prayers of the Church are abolished, but now there are very many who never pray at all. ...I have never entered their conventicles, but I have sometimes seen them returning from their sermons, the countenances of all of them displaying rage, and wonderful ferocity, as though they were animated by the evil spirit. ...Who ever beheld in their meetings any one of them shedding tears, smiting his breast, or grieving for his sins?"
